staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced the bug against this preserved vulnerable checkout. The saved AddressSanitizer trace reaches `zend_string_release()` at `Zend/zend_string.h:319` from `zend_closure_free_storage()` at `Zend/zend_closures.c:486`, and the staged patch adds the missing internal-closure `function_name` ownership fixes in this exact tree.

classification.classification_note: The reproduced failure is an AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free read. A trampoline-backed callable built from the attacker-controlled PHP method string is copied into two closure objects without incrementing the shared `zend_string` refcount; destroying the unused `bindTo()` result frees that string first, and destroying the original temporary closure immediately afterwards re-enters `zend_string_release()` on the same freed allocation.

bug_description.original: Heap-use-after-free in Zend/zend_closures.c: zend_closure_free_storage can end up invoking zend_string_release on a function name that has already been freed, causing subsequent reads of freed heap memory (seen via zend_string_release and zend_objects_store_del). This use-after-free during closure/object destruction can cause crashes, memory corruption and may be exploitable for information disclosure or arbitrary code execution.
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01's saved run executed the exact staged `poc` under `./sapi/cli/php /gt/poc` and reached `Closure::fromCallable([$foo, "\x00"])->bindTo(new Foo)` on a class that only implements `__call`. On the witnessed path `zend_std_get_method()` cannot find the requested method and therefore builds a trampoline function for `__call`; because the attacker-controlled method string contains an embedded NUL byte, `zend_get_call_trampoline_func()` takes the `zend_string_init(..., mname_len, 0)` branch and allocates a dedicated zero-length `function_name` string for that trampoline. `zend_create_closure_from_callable()` then wraps the trampoline as a stack `zend_internal_function call`, and `zend_create_fake_closure()` copies that internal function into the first closure object. Vulnerable `zend_create_closure_ex()` does not add a refcount for internal-function `function_name`, so the first closure only borrows the same string allocation. `Closure::bindTo()` then calls `zend_create_closure()` on that first closure and vulnerable `zend_create_closure_ex()` copies the same borrowed pointer into the second closure, again without a refcount increment. When the chained expression finishes, the `bindTo()` return value is unused, so `i_zval_ptr_dtor()` destroys that second closure first and `zend_closure_free_storage()` releases the shared `function_name`, freeing the heap string. The VM then releases the original temporary receiver closure, `zend_closure_free_storage()` calls `zend_string_release()` on the stale pointer again, and the saved AddressSanitizer trace reports the resulting read of the freed `zend_string` header at `Zend/zend_string.h:319`.

source.description: First project statement that materializes attacker-controlled data into the vulnerable heap object. For a missing method on an object with `__call`, this branch allocates the trampoline-owned `zend_string` later aliased by both closures and then freed twice.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` bytes show the callable is `[$foo, "\x00"]`: `od` on `gt_results/secbench_oss_php.ossfuzz-42500752/poc` contains `... 5b 24 66 6f 6f 2c 22 00 22 5d ...`. Because the method string contains an embedded NUL, `strlen(ZSTR_VAL(method_name))` becomes `0` while `ZSTR_LEN(method_name)` is `1`, so this statement allocates the exact zero-length `zend_string` that later becomes dangling.

sink.description: Crash sink. The second closure teardown passes the already freed `function_name` pointer into `zend_string_release()`, and the first read of the freed `zend_string` header occurs here when `ZSTR_IS_INTERNED(s)` inspects `GC_FLAGS(s)`.

root_cause.description: Root cause fixed by the patch. Internal closure creation copies the borrowed `function_name` pointer from `func` into the closure without incrementing the underlying `zend_string` refcount, so multiple closures can later release the same allocation as though each owned it. The patch adds the missing `zend_string_addref(closure->func.op_array.function_name);` in this branch and then balances temporary trampoline wrappers with explicit releases after closure creation.

tainted_value_origin.description: The attacker-controlled PHP method string `"\x00"` is first turned into the trampoline `function_name` object here. Every later alias, refcount decision, free, and stale release in the vulnerability chain refers back to this same heap `zend_string` allocation.

parser_admitted.description: The staged PHP program has been parsed and is executing the attacker-controlled callable expression. Method lookup has accepted the object/method input and entered the missing-method branch used by the issue-relevant __call trampoline path.

coarse_trace.summary: Resolving the missing method on an object with `__call` creates a trampoline function whose `function_name` heap string is derived from the attacker-controlled method bytes `"\x00"`.

The trampoline-backed callable is wrapped as an internal closure for `Closure::fromCallable`, but internal closure creation copies the `function_name` pointer without taking a `zend_string` reference.
Calling `bindTo()` on that first closure creates a second internal closure that aliases the same borrowed `function_name` pointer, again without a refcount increment.
Because the chained expression result is unused, the VM destroys the `bindTo()` return value first, and its closure destructor releases and frees the shared `function_name` string.

The VM then releases the original temporary receiver closure, which tries to release the same already freed `function_name` pointer and triggers the saved heap-use-after-free read in `zend_string_release()`.

fine_trace.note: Resolving the callable method name from `[$foo, "\x00"]` misses in the class function table. Because the class defines `__call`, this branch takes the fallback into `zend_get_user_call_function()`, which is the only path that reaches the trampoline allocation below.

Source. The `__call` fallback materializes attacker-controlled method bytes into a trampoline-owned heap `zend_string`. Because the method contains an embedded NUL, `strlen(ZSTR_VAL(method_name))` yields `0` while `ZSTR_LEN(method_name)` is `1`, so this branch allocates the exact zero-length `function_name` object later aliased by both closures.

The trampoline-backed callable path wraps the resolved trampoline as a stack `zend_internal_function call` by aliasing the same `function_name` pointer into `call.function_name` before creating a closure from it.
For `Closure::fromCallable([$foo, "\x00"])`, the trampoline-backed internal function from step 3 is passed into closure creation as the callable body for the first temporary closure object.

Root cause. Creating the first closure copies the internal function, including `function_name`, into `closure->func` without incrementing the `zend_string` refcount. The closure therefore only borrows the allocation from step 2 instead of owning a distinct reference.

Calling `bindTo(new Foo)` on the first closure reuses that closure's internal-function descriptor as the source for a second closure object, so the same borrowed `function_name` pointer is about to be copied again.

The `bindTo()` result closure receives the same `function_name` pointer through the same refcount-less internal-copy path. After this step, both closure objects alias one heap `zend_string` allocation whose reference count still reflects only a single owner.

Because the `bindTo()` return value is unused, `i_zval_ptr_dtor(ret)` destroys that second closure first. Its destructor takes the internal-closure cleanup branch and calls `zend_string_release()` on the shared `function_name` pointer.

The first destructor decrements the shared string's only counted reference to zero and frees the heap allocation. The saved free stack shows this happens during `i_zval_ptr_dtor()` before the later crashing release.

After freeing the unused return value, the VM releases the original temporary receiver closure. Its destructor takes the same internal-closure branch and passes the same now-dangling `function_name` pointer to `zend_string_release()` again.
Sink. The second release reads the freed `zend_string` header while evaluating `ZSTR_IS_INTERNED(s)`, producing the saved AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free read at `Zend/zend_string.h:319`.

sanitizer_ground_truth.patch_resolves_note: The staged patch is source-consistent with this root cause because it adds the missing internal-closure `zend_string_addref()` and balances temporary trampoline wrappers with explicit `zend_string_release()` calls in both `zend_create_closure_from_callable()` and `zend_closure_from_frame()`. Stage 02 did not execute the fixed build, so this field does not claim dynamic confirmation.

format.name: PHP source file
format.contract: The verified trigger is the exact staged witness at `gt_results/secbench_oss_php.ossfuzz-42500752/poc`. Its load-bearing properties are: the file defines a class with `__call`; it evaluates `Closure::fromCallable([$foo, "\x00"])->bindTo(new Foo)`; method resolution therefore takes the `__call` trampoline path on the exact embedded-NUL method string `"\x00"`; and the overall chained expression result is unused, so the temporary `bindTo()` result closure is destroyed before the original temporary closure.
